lead: The three piston-engine cycles differ in one thing only: how the heat goes in. The Otto cycle adds it at constant volume, as if a spark burned the charge instantly at top dead centre; it models the petrol engine. The Diesel cycle adds it at constant pressure while the piston moves out, as fuel injected into hot air burns steadily; it models the slow-speed compression-ignition engine. The Dual cycle adds part at constant volume and the rest at constant pressure, which is closer to a modern high-speed diesel. Each gives an efficiency formula in terms of the compression ratio and one or two more ratios.
prereq: You need the air standard assumptions and the process relations from Air standard cycles and their assumptions.

sections.h3: Otto cycle: heat added at constant volume

blocks.text: State 1 is the start of compression. The processes are 1→2 isentropic compression, 2→3 heat addition at constant volume, 3→4 isentropic expansion and 4→1 heat rejection at constant volume. The compression ratio is r = v₁/v₂, the total volume over the clearance volume; since v₃ = v₂ and v₄ = v₁, the expansion ratio is also r.

items: Heat added q<sub>in</sub> = c<sub>v</sub>(T₃ − T₂); heat rejected q<sub>out</sub> = c<sub>v</sub>(T₄ − T₁).
Isentropic steps: T₂ = T₁r<sup>γ−1</sup> and T₃ = T₄r<sup>γ−1</sup>, so T₃ − T₂ = r<sup>γ−1</sup>(T₄ − T₁).

blocks.text: ηOtto = 1 − 1/rγ−1. It depends only on r and γ, not on how much heat is added. Raising r raises η, but a petrol engine compresses the fuel-air mixture, and above r of about 10 to 12 the mixture can self-ignite before the spark (knock). That limit, not thermodynamics, keeps the petrol engine's r low.

sections.h3: Diesel cycle: heat added at constant pressure

blocks.text: The Diesel cycle keeps 1→2 isentropic compression, 3→4 isentropic expansion and 4→1 constant-volume rejection, but heat goes in at constant pressure from 2 to 3. The cut-off ratio is rc = v₃/v₂ = T₃/T₂, the volume at which fuel injection ends divided by the clearance volume. When cut-off is given as a fraction k of the stroke, v₃ − v₂ = k(v₁ − v₂), so rc = 1 + k(r − 1).

items: q<sub>in</sub> = c<sub>p</sub>(T₃ − T₂) because the pressure is constant; q<sub>out</sub> = c<sub>v</sub>(T₄ − T₁).
T₂ = T₁r<sup>γ−1</sup>, T₃ = r<sub>c</sub>T₂, and expansion from v₃ to v₄ = v₁ gives T₄ = T₃(r<sub>c</sub>/r)<sup>γ−1</sup> = T₁r<sub>c</sub><sup>γ</sup>.

blocks.text: ηDiesel = 1 − (1/rγ−1) × (rcγ − 1)/[γ(rc − 1)]. The bracket is always greater than 1 when rc > 1, so at the same r a Diesel cycle is less efficient than an Otto cycle, and its efficiency falls as cut-off gets later (more load). A diesel engine compresses only air, so knock does not limit r; it runs at r of about 14 to 22 and ends up more efficient in practice.

sections.h3: Dual cycle: heat added in two parts

blocks.text: The Dual (mixed, or limited-pressure) cycle has five processes: 1→2 isentropic compression, 2→3 heat at constant volume, 3→4 heat at constant pressure, 4→5 isentropic expansion and 5→1 rejection at constant volume. It needs two more ratios: the pressure ratio rp = p₃/p₂ (also called the explosion ratio) and the cut-off ratio rc = v₄/v₃. Note that in the Dual cycle cut-off is measured from state 3, not state 2.

q<sub>in</sub> = c<sub>v</sub>(T₃ − T₂) + c<sub>p</sub>(T₄ − T₃), q<sub>out</sub> = c<sub>v</sub>(T₅ − T₁), with T₃ = r<sub>p</sub>T₂, T₄ = r<sub>c</sub>T₃ and T₅ = T₁r<sub>p</sub>r<sub>c</sub><sup>γ</sup>. The result is

Put rc = 1 and the formula becomes the Otto formula; put rp = 1 and it becomes the Diesel formula. So the Dual cycle contains the other two as its limits, and its efficiency lies between them for the same r and heat input. A full Dual cycle calculation, with mean effective pressure, is worked in Air standard efficiency, mean effective pressure, comparison.

examples.question: An air standard Otto cycle has a compression ratio of 8. At the start of compression the air is at 1 bar and 300 K, and 800 kJ/kg of heat is added per cycle. Take c<sub>v</sub> = 0.718 kJ/kg·K, R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K and γ = 1.4. Find the temperatures and pressures at all states, the efficiency and the net work.
steps: Volumes: v₁ = 0.287 × 300/100 = 0.861 m³/kg and v₂ = v₁/8 = 0.1076 m³/kg.
Heat at constant volume: T₃ = T₂ + q<sub>in</sub>/c<sub>v</sub> = 689.2 + 800/0.718 = 689.2 + 1114.2 = 1803.4 K. p₃ = p₂T₃/T₂ = 18.38 × 2.617 = 48.09 bar.
Expansion: T₄ = T₃/r<sup>γ−1</sup> = 1803.4/2.297 = 785.0 K. p₄ = p₁T₄/T₁ = 785.0/300 = 2.62 bar.

examples.question: An air standard Diesel cycle has a compression ratio of 15, and fuel cut-off occurs at 6% of the stroke. The air is at 1 bar and 300 K at the start of compression. Take c<sub>p</sub> = 1.005 and c<sub>v</sub> = 0.718 kJ/kg·K, γ = 1.4. Find the cut-off ratio, the temperatures, the heat added and rejected, and the efficiency.
examples.answer: r<sub>c</sub> = 1.84; T₂ = 886.3 K, T₃ = 1630.7 K, T₄ = 704.5 K; q<sub>in</sub> = 748.2 kJ/kg, q<sub>out</sub> = 290.4 kJ/kg; η = 61.2%.

traps: Cut-off ratio is v₃/v₂ in the Diesel cycle but v₄/v₃ in the Dual cycle, because the Dual cycle's constant-pressure part starts at state 3. Read the state numbers before using a formula.
"Cut-off at 6% of the stroke" means r<sub>c</sub> = 1 + 0.06(r − 1), not 1.06 and not 0.06r.
Use c<sub>p</sub> for heat added at constant pressure and c<sub>v</sub> for heat at constant volume. Using c<sub>v</sub> for the Diesel heat input makes q<sub>in</sub> 29% too small.
Keep temperatures in kelvin. A question that gives 27 °C at the start of compression means T₁ = 300 K; putting 27 into T₂ = T₁r<sup>γ−1</sup> gives 62 K instead of 689 K.
The Otto formula 1 − 1/r<sup>γ−1</sup> is not the Diesel efficiency. For the same r the Diesel value is lower; the Diesel engine wins in practice only because it can use a higher r.

quiz.q: Name the processes of the Dual cycle in order.
quiz.a: 1→2 isentropic compression, 2→3 constant-volume heat addition, 3→4 constant-pressure heat addition, 4→5 isentropic expansion, 5→1 constant-volume heat rejection.

quiz.q: Why does the Diesel cycle use c<sub>p</sub> for heat added but c<sub>v</sub> for heat rejected?
quiz.a: Heat is added from 2 to 3 at constant pressure, so q = c<sub>p</sub>ΔT; it is rejected from 4 to 1 at constant volume, so q = c<sub>v</sub>ΔT.

quiz.q: Why can a diesel engine use a much higher compression ratio than a petrol engine?
quiz.a: A diesel engine compresses only air and injects fuel at the end, so nothing can self-ignite early. A petrol engine compresses a fuel-air mixture, which knocks above r of about 10 to 12.

quiz.q: Find the air standard efficiency of an Otto cycle with r = 6 (γ = 1.4).
A Diesel cycle has r = 16 and r<sub>c</sub> = 2. Find its efficiency (γ = 1.4).
Show that the Dual cycle efficiency becomes the Diesel efficiency when r<sub>p</sub> = 1.
quiz.a: With r<sub>p</sub> = 1 the numerator r<sub>p</sub>r<sub>c</sub><sup>γ</sup> − 1 becomes r<sub>c</sub><sup>γ</sup> − 1 and the denominator (r<sub>p</sub> − 1) + γr<sub>p</sub>(r<sub>c</sub> − 1) becomes γ(r<sub>c</sub> − 1). That is the Diesel formula.

quiz.q: In the Diesel example, cut-off moves from 6% to 10% of the stroke at the same r. Does the efficiency rise or fall? Find it.
quiz.a: r<sub>c</sub> = 1 + 0.1 × 14 = 2.4; 2.4<sup>1.4</sup> = 3.406. η = 1 − (1/2.954)(2.406/1.96) = 1 − 0.416 = 0.584. It falls from 61.2% to 58.4%: later cut-off means more heat at lower efficiency.

beyond: Real engines do not burn at constant volume or constant pressure. Engine researchers fit a smooth heat-release curve (the Wiebe function) to measured cylinder pressure. Modern petrol engines push the compression ratio up with direct injection, and some use a late-closing intake valve (the Atkinson or Miller cycle) to expand further than they compress. Search for "Wiebe function", "Miller cycle" and "Atkinson cycle hybrid engine" to see where these cycles go next.
